title: Do penguin species differ in flipper length?
text:
Code: read the data and compute the numbers
library(tidyverse)

penguins <- read_csv("../data/example/penguins.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Mean flipper length per species (2 penguins have no measurement)
flipper_means <- penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm)) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(mean_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm))

mean_of <- function(sp) flipper_means %>% filter(species == sp) %>% pull(mean_mm)
gentoo_vs_chinstrap_mm <- mean_of("Gentoo") - mean_of("Chinstrap")
gentoo_vs_adelie_mm <- mean_of("Gentoo") - mean_of("Adelie")

n_penguins <- nrow(penguins)
n_islands <- n_distinct(penguins$island)
n_no_flipper <- sum(is.na(penguins$flipper_length_mm))
first_year <- min(penguins$year)
last_year <- max(penguins$year)




Code: make the figure
set.seed(3901)  # same jitter on every render
penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Gentoo penguins have the longest flippers",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Flipper length (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Figure 1: Flipper length by species. Each point is one penguin; each box shows the middle half of a species, and the line inside it is the median.





Finding. Gentoo penguins have the longest flippers, on average about 21 mm longer than Chinstrap and 27 mm longer than Adelie penguins.
Limitation. These are 344 penguins measured on 3 islands near Palmer Station, Antarctica, in 2007–2009; 2 have no flipper measurement.
Data source. Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data (R package). https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/ License: CC0.

title: Guided Project: Statistical Transformations and Coordinate Systems
text:
Part A · Fairness
My group: Age My outcome: time_in_hospital >= 5.
Question A: “Of each age group, what share has the outcome of time_in_hospital >= 5?” Question B: “Of everyone with time_in_hospital >= 5, what share is each age group?”

A0 · My group and my outcome

a_data <- fairness %>%
  mutate(
    group = age,
    has_outcome = time_in_hospital >= 5
  )

a_data %>%
  count(group, has_outcome) %>%
  print(n = Inf)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  group               has_outcome     n
  <chr>               <lgl>       <int>
1 30 years or younger FALSE         106
2 30 years or younger TRUE           35
3 30-60 years         FALSE        1012
4 30-60 years         TRUE          499
5 Over 60 years       FALSE        1962
6 Over 60 years       TRUE         1386




A1 · The rate within each group (question A)

a1 <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the group", y = NULL, fill = "Has the outcome")

show_plot(a1)







Figure 1: Share of each group with the outcome.





I would guess that older people would have a longer time in the hospital, so I expect the highest rate to be in the older age groups. The plot shows that people over 60 have the highest share of time_in_hospital >= 5, while people under 30 have the lowest share. People between 30 and 60 years sit in between. This makes groups of different sizes comparable because it brings all groups to the same scale instead of being different just because there is more people in one group or the other.


A2 · Rates with their standard error

a2_rates <- a_data %>%
  drop_na(has_outcome) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    rate = mean(has_outcome),
    se = sqrt(rate * (1-rate) / n)
  )

a2 <- ggplot(a2_rates,
             aes(x = rate, y = group,
                 xmin = rate - se,
                 xmax = rate + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  # Many groups, and the labels touch the points? Keep every group, and use
  # vjust = -0.8, size = 3 instead of nudge_y = 0.3.
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Rate (share of the group with the outcome)", y = NULL)

show_plot(a2)







Figure 2: Rate in each group, with ± one standard error and the group size.





The youngest group has the widest range. It tells the reader that even though the group is small, it has a high variability in th e outcome. One or two outliers can already have a significant impact on the results.


A3 · Zoom or filter?

a3_table <- a_data %>%
  count(group) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
a3_table

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  group                   n
  <chr>               <int>
1 Over 60 years        3348
2 30-60 years          1511
3 30 years or younger   141

a3_start <- 120

a3_counts <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Count", y = NULL)

a3_zoom <- a3_counts +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(a3_start, max(a3_table$n)), expand = FALSE)

# A warning about removed rows here is expected (Session 2, slide 5).
a3_filter <- a3_counts +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(a3_start, max(a3_table$n)))

# Lie Factor (Tufte, 2001, p. 57) of the zoomed plot, largest vs smallest
# group: how many times the picture exaggerates the difference.
a3_largest <- max(a3_table$n)
a3_smallest <- min(a3_table$n)
a3_lie_factor <-
  ((a3_largest - a3_start) / (a3_smallest - a3_start)) /
  (a3_largest / a3_smallest)
a3_lie_factor

[1] 6.47363

show_plot(a3_counts)
show_plot(a3_zoom)
show_plot(a3_filter)











(a) From 0











(b) Zoomed











(c) Filtered







Figure 3: Counts per group: from 0, zoomed and filtered.




The zoomed plot’s Lie Factor (largest vs smallest group) is 6.5.
The first version shows the full picture with a normal scale and the whole x axis is shown from 0 up to a little more than the biggest group has. The second plot starts just slightly above the amount of the smallest group. This makes the smallest group look even less represented and is quite misleading. The third plot filters out all of the data and is therefore empty.


A4 · Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome (question B)

a4_shares <- a_data %>%
  filter(has_outcome) %>%
  count(group) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

a4 <- ggplot(a4_shares, aes(x = share, y = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Share of everyone with the outcome", y = NULL)

show_plot(a4)







Figure 4: Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome.





They do point in the same direction since the plots always confirm each other. Already in the beginning, the oldest group stood out which was then confirmed throughout.

title: Guided Project: Statistical Transformations and Coordinate Systems
text:
Part B · Sports
My group, outcome and value: group = the number of of sets played in the match, outcome = the home player won, value = the total points sccored in game 1.

  mutate(
    group = factor(Sets_P1 + Sets_P2),
    has_outcome = HomeWinner == 1,
    value = P1_G1 + P2_G1
  )

b_data %>%
  count(group, has_outcome) %>%
  print(n = Inf)

B1 · The rate within each group

b1 <- ggplot(b_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the group", y = "Sets played", fill = "Home player won")

show_plot(b1)







Figure 5: Share of each group with the outcome.





The home player won about 50% of the matches (50.1%) in the 3-set matches, 49.5% in the 4-set matches, and 49.4% in the 5-set matches, so the link of the matches shows almost no connection to who wins. I use shares because the groups are of different sizes and it makes them comparable.


B2 · A mean with its two spreads

b2_summary <- b_data %>%
  drop_na(value) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(value),
    sd = sd(value),
    se = sd / sqrt(n)
  )

b2 <- ggplot(b2_summary,
             aes(x = mean, y = group,
                 xmin = mean - se,
                 xmax = mean + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Mean points in game 1", y = "Sets played")


show_plot(b2)







Figure 6: Mean in each group, with ± one standard error and group size.

The mean of game 1 is about 18.5 points for 3-set matches and about 18.8 points for 4- and 5-set matches, a gap of about 0.3 points. This gap is large compared to the se (each bar is only about ±0.06 points wide, and the 3-set bar does not overlap the other two), so it is unlikely to be just sampling noise. We should take from this that there is a small, fairly clear difference between the averages, not a difference that would let anyone predict the length of a match from its first game.


B3 · Zoom or filter?

b3_table <- b_data %>%
  count(group) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
b3_table

  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Count", y = "Sets played")

b3_zoom <- b3_counts +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(b3_start, max(b3_table$n)), expand = FALSE)

b3_filter <- b3_counts +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(b3_start, max(b3_table$n)))

b3_lie_factor <-
  ((max(b3_table$n) - b3_start) / (min(b3_table$n) - b3_start)) /
  (max(b3_table$n) / min(b3_table$n))
b3_lie_factor

[1] 1.177998

show_plot(b3_zoom)

(a) Zoomed











(b) Filtered







Figure 7: Counts per group: zoomed and filtered.




The Lie Factor of your zoomed plot is 1.18. The zoomed plot makes the 4 matches seem much more common than the other two even though they are pretty close. The filtered version removes the bars completely because they start at 0, which is outside of the limits.


B4 · Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome

b4_shares <- b_data %>%
  filter(has_outcome) %>%
  count(group) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

b4 <- ggplot(b4_shares, aes(x = share, y = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Share of all home wins", y = "Sets played")

show_plot(b4)







Figure 8: Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome.





B4 does not point in the same direction as B1. B1 shows almost no difference while B4 shows that 4-set matches have the largest share. This is more likely because there are more 4-set matches in total, so they make up the biggest part of the home wins just because they are the biggest group.

A0 · See it update

show_plot(a0)







Figure 1: My first plot: a count of one of my Fairness columns.





Yes, I changed one word in the title of a0 in the script, and the new title shows up both here and in my slides.


A1 · Label it

a_data <- fairness %>%
  mutate(
    group = age,
    has_outcome = time_in_hospital >= 5
  )

a_data %>%
  count(group, has_outcome) %>%
  print(n = Inf)

  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the group", y = NULL, fill = "Has the outcome")

a1 <- a1_base +
  labs(
    title = "Longer hospital stays are more common in older age groups ",
    subtitle = "From the Diabetes Hospital encounters dataset",
    x = "Share of the age group in %",
    y = "Age Group",
    fill = "Stay of 5+ days"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent)

show_plot(a1)







Figure 2: Share of each group with the outcome, labeled for a reader.





I changed the title most. The first version only named the topic, and now it says what a reader can see in the plot. The subtitle names the data, and the axis and legend titles explain the share and the outcome (a stay of 5 or more days), so a reader can understand the plot without me there.


A2 · Choose a scale

a2 <- NULL
# YOUR TURN: remove the # signs below, then replace each ___.
a2 <- fairness %>%
  filter(time_in_hospital > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = time_in_hospital)) +

  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Most hospital stays are short and only a few last two weeks",
       x = "Time in hospital (days)",
       y = "Number of encounters (log scale)")


# YOUR TURN: one sentence. Why this scale for this column?
a2_reason <- "Time in hospital is right-skewed, with many short stays and a few long ones, so a log scale represents this data better. "

show_plot(a2)







Figure 3: My scale choice.





I used a log scale on the y-axis (the number of encounters) because the stay lengths are right-skewed: short stays are common and long ones are rare. With the log scale a reader can see that even the rare long stays (about 45 encounters at 14 days) are present next to the common ones (about 870 at 3 days). The trade-off is that the bars start at 1 instead of 0, so their lengths no longer show the counts directly, and a linear scale shows the skew more clearly. No values were removed by the filter (0 rows had a stay of 0 days or less).


A3 · Facet it: fixed or free

  mutate(panel = paste0(panel, " (n = ", scales::comma(panel_n), ")")) %>%
  group_by(panel, group) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), rate = mean(has_outcome), .groups = "drop")

a3_free <- NULL

  scale_x_discrete(labels = scales::label_wrap(10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Share with a stay of 5+ days, by age group and race",
       x = "Age group", y = "Share of the group (%)")
a3_free <- a3_fixed +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel), scales = "free_y")


# YOUR TURN 3: which one would you publish, "fixed" or "free_y"? Why?
a3_choice <- "fixed"
a3_reason <- "With the same y-axis in every panel, a reader can compare the rates across panels more easily and is not overwhelmed with information. Also, the smaller panels are not stretched to look as important as the big ones."

A4 · Compared to what?

I chose the number of lab procedures per encounter, because it is a count with a wide spread. The individual values of the two genders overlap almost completely, from about 1 to 70 procedures, while the 200 resampled means form narrow bands around 16 that sit only slightly apart. This means the group means are measured precisely, but the gap between them is small compared with the differences between single encounters, so knowing the gender says very little about one encounter. I left out the 2 encounters with unknown gender, because a resampled mean of 2 values would not mean much.

text:
Part B · Sports

B1 · Label it

b_data <- sports %>%
  mutate(
    group = factor(Sets_P1 + Sets_P2),
    has_outcome = HomeWinner == 1,
    value = P1_G1 + P2_G1
  )

b1_base <- ggplot(b_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Share of the group", y = "Sets played", fill = "Home player won")

b1 <- b1_base +
  labs(
    title = "The home player wins about half of all matches, however long they last",
    subtitle = "From the Setka Cup table tennis matches dataset",
    x = "Share of matches (%)",
    y = "Home player won"
  )

show_plot(b1)







Figure 8: My Sports plot, labeled for a reader.





The plot shows that the home player won about 50% of the matches in every group, whether the match lasted 3, 4 or 5 sets. The title helps a reader most, because it states this finding instead of only naming the columns.


B2 · Choose a scale

b2 <- b_data %>%
  filter(value > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, color = "black") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Points in game 1: most games end near 18, a few run much longer",
       subtitle="The bars that fall below 1 are bins with just 1 observation",
       x = "Points in game 1 (both players)", y = "Matches (log scale)")

b2_reason <- "The points in game 1 are right-skewed, with many games ending near 18 points and a few running much longer, so a log scale represents this data better without making the shorter data points seem extremely large."

show_plot(b2)







Figure 9: My scale choice.





used a log scale on the y-axis (the number of matches). The points in game 1 are right-skewed: most games end near 18 points, and a few long games with many deuces run much higher, up to 44 points. On a linear count axis the bars for the rare long games would be almost invisible next to the tall bars near 18. The log scale makes these rare games visible, and it does not make the common short games look extremely large. The trade-off is that the bars on a log axis no longer show the counts directly, and bins with only 1 match have a bar of length zero, which is why some bars seem to be missing (the subtitle explains this). No values were removed, because every game has at least 11 points (0 rows removed).


B3 · Facet it: fixed or free

b3_fixed <- NULL
b3_free <- NULL

b3_rates <- b_data %>%
  mutate(panel = if_else(HomeWinner == 1, "Home player won", "Away player won")) %>%
  add_count(panel, name = "panel_n") %>%
  mutate(panel = paste0(panel, " (n = ", scales::comma(panel_n), ")")) %>%
  group_by(panel, group) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), mean_points = mean(value), .groups = "drop")

b3_fixed <- ggplot(b3_rates, aes(x = group, y = mean_points)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel)) +
  labs(title = "Mean points in game 1, by sets played and who won",
       x = "Sets played", y = "Mean points in game 1")
b3_free <- b3_fixed +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel), scales = "free_y")


b3_choice <- "fixed"
b3_reason <- "Both panels have means between about 18 and 19 points, so free axes give no extra detail, while fixed axes keep the two panels directly comparable and show that who won the match makes almost no difference to game 1."

show_plot(b3_fixed)
show_plot(b3_free)











(a) Fixed











(b) Free







Figure 10: The same plot in panels: fixed and free y-axes.




I chose fixed axes. The two versions look almost the same, because bars start at 0 and all the means are between about 18 and 19 points, so free axes add no detail. Fixed axes keep the two panels directly comparable and show that who won the match makes almost no difference to the mean of game 1. Both panels are large (n = 3,952 for the away player and n = 3,899 for the home player), so there is no small-panel problem here. In both panels the means for 4 and 5 sets are slightly higher than for 3 sets, by a few tenths of a point.


B4 · Compared to what?

b4_clouds <- b_data %>%
  mutate(winner = if_else(HomeWinner == 1, "Home player won", "Away player won")) %>%
  make_clouds(winner, value)

b4 <- ggplot(b4_clouds, aes(x = group, y = value)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ kind) +
  labs(title = "Points in game 1: individual matches versus group means",
       x = "Who won the match", y = "Points in game 1 (both players)")

show_plot(b4)







Figure 11: Two groups: individual values and resampled means, same axes.





The clouds of the two groups overlap almost completely, both for the individual values and for the resampled means. The individual games range from 11 to 44 points, while the resampled means form narrow bands near 18.7 points. This means the group means are measured precisely, but the difference between them, if there is one, is tiny compared with the differences between single games, so who won the match tells us almost nothing about the points in game 1.


B5 · Color for every reader
b5 <- ggplot(b_data, aes(y = group, fill = group)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Matches by number of sets played", x = "Matches",
       y = "Sets played", fill = "Sets played")

show_plot(b5)
show_plot(simulate_plot(b5, "Red-green (deuteranopia)"))











(a) My plot











(b) Red-green (deuteranopia), simulated







Figure 12: My colors, with a second cue, and how a reader with red-green color blindness might see them.

the blue-yellow one is an approximation.

  <chr>                                   <dbl> <chr>      
1 Red-green (deuteranopia)                 30.5 Yes

3 Blue-yellow (approximate)                29.7 Yes        


show_plot(simulate_plot(b5, "Red-green (protanopia)"))
show_plot(simulate_plot(b5, "Blue-yellow (approximate)"))











(a) Red-green (protanopia), simulated











(b) Blue-yellow (approximate), simulated







Figure 13: The other two simulated views.



I colored the bars by the number of sets played, which has three categories (3, 4 and 5), so each can get its own viridis color. The sets are also on the y-axis, so color is not the only cue. In the simulated plots I can still tell the three bars apart.

For the limits, I added one slide that says what the data can and cannot show, for example that the home-win rate says nothing about a real home advantage, because the home player may only be the first-listed player. This helps a reader judge how far to trust the finding.

text:
What it shows, and its limits

The share of long stays differs by age group, and the pattern looks the same for all of the races. This describes a difference, not a cause.
A stay of 5 or more days is my own cutoff, and the data cover US hospitals from 1999 to 2008, so they say nothing about today.
In the Sports data, “home player” probably only means the first-listed player, so a 50% win rate is not evidence for a real home advantage.
